metadata.title: Compiling Is Not Migrating.
metadata.youtube_title: Compiling Is Not Migrating — An Overview of My SQL Server to Snowflake Migration

beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Hussain, and this video is about my current migration project: moving a SQL Server financial planning database onto Snowflake, and building the tools that prove the move actually worked, not just that it compiled.

show.event: composer card settles, greeting 'Salaam, Hussain' fades in
the ask types into the composer
send arms terracotta; running indicator reads 'reading Main.sql…'
three result lines stagger in beneath — the ask lands answered

props.command: I am moving a SQL Server financial planning database to Snowflake. The converted script is one 1,244-line file. Split it into something deployable, find what will not run on Snowflake, and tell me how I will prove the data and the procedures still behave the same.
output: a linter for SQL Server habits, with fixes

beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW — opens on the Claude UI; the ask lands answered. The intro line follows the human's requested pattern.

beats.narration_text: Here is the whole idea. A migration is not a translation, it is a proof that nothing changed. Getting the SQL to compile is where the work starts, not where it ends.

show.event: line one types: 'Migrating is translating.'
'translating' turns terracotta, deletes, 'proving' types in
'Compiling is done.' types
'done' turns terracotta and corrects to 'the start'
the corrected overview holds complete: Migrating is proving. Compiling is the start.

props.text:
Migrating is translating.
Compiling is done.

beats.role_note: EXECUTIVE-SUMMARY LAW — corrects the misconception (migration as translation; compile = done) to the claim the body argues (a proof; compiling is the start).

beats.narration_text: It started as one file. Twelve hundred and forty four lines of converted SQL, plus a folder of procedures that had drifted out of sync with it. So I split it. One object per file, eight stages, numbered in the order they have to deploy. Then I checked nothing was lost. Thirty two create statements went in, thirty two came out.

show.event: a tall Main.sql card; its line counter runs up to 1,244
a dashed tag lands beneath it: 'procedures/ — drifted out of sync'
eight stage folders fill in deploy order with file counts; the file's lines thin as they go
the verdict lands under a terracotta rule: '32 of 32 CREATE statements · each exactly once'

props.verdict: 32 of 32 CREATE statements · each exactly once
props.footnote: Source: snowshift repo · sql/ and manifest.yaml

beats.narration_text: The first tool is a linter. Twenty seven rules, each one a SQL Server habit that Snowflake either rejects outright or quietly reads differently, and every rule carries the fix, not just the complaint. It paid for itself on day one. A select top ten, hiding in the sample data script, that would have failed the moment it ran.

show.event: '27' lands large with 'DIALECT RULES · EACH WITH ITS FIX' and three severity chips
four T-SQL habits appear one by one; each is struck and its Snowflake fix appears beside it
a terracotta-bordered card rises: the real catch in the seed script
'SELECT TOP 10 …' is struck in terracotta; 'ORDER BY … LIMIT 10' lands

props.catchLabel: Found on day one · would fail on execution

beats.narration_text: Then deployment. Here is the ask: run the files in order, dry run first, stop at the first failure, and never load sample data into production.

show.event: composer returns; greeting slot reads 'The ask,'
the deploy prompt types itself in
send arms terracotta; running indicator reads 'planning the deployment…'
no output lines — the result is the next beat (ASK then RESULT)

props.command: Deploy these 29 files to Snowflake in manifest order. Dry-run first. If a file fails, stop there and mark everything after it skipped. Never load the sample data in a production run.

beats.narration_text: And this is what comes back. Six required stages run in dependency order, setup through procedures. Seed data and tests are optional, so a production cutover can never load sample rows by accident. And when a file fails, the run stops right there. In an ordered deploy, everything after the first failure is just noise.

show.event: six required stage cards tick 'ok' in manifest order
the two optional stages turn dashed: 'not in prod'
the run replays: 'views' is stamped FAIL
everything after it greys to 'skipped'
the rule lands under a terracotta dash

props.optionalLabel: optional · never in a production run
props.rule: Stop at the first failure. The rest is noise.
props.footnote: The failure shown is illustrative · snowshift deploy

beats.narration_text: Then parity. For every table, row counts plus count, sum, min and max on the columns that matter, using only aggregates that mean the same thing on both engines. And the columns are declared, not discovered. A decimal that quietly landed as a float looks identical if you only introspect. Then it drifts, one rounding error at a time.

show.event: three aggregate rows land pairwise — SQL Server value, tick, Snowflake value
a fourth row lands: CostCenter · SUM(AllocationPercentage)
its Snowflake value diverges; the ≠ mark and border turn terracotta
two lenses: introspected passes, declared fails — DECIMAL(19,4) → FLOAT

props.lensIntrospect: Introspected: FLOAT matches FLOAT, so it passes.

beats.narration_text: This is the one that worried me most. Snowflake lets you declare primary keys and unique constraints, and then does not enforce them. SQL Server rejected a duplicate budget line the moment you wrote it. Snowflake just stores it. So run the same import twice, and the budget doubles. No error, anywhere.

show.event: the real natural-key constraint types into a code strip
two panels: SQL Server 'enforced at write time' · Snowflake 'declared · not enforced'
import run 1 lands on both sides, ticked
run 2: SQL Server stamps REJECTED; Snowflake stamps STORED
Snowflake's budget total grows from 1× to 2× in terracotta

props.constraint: ALTER TABLE Planning.BudgetLineItem ADD CONSTRAINT idx_BudgetLineItem_NaturalKey UNIQUE (BudgetHeaderID, GLAccountID, CostCenterID, FiscalPeriodID);

beats.narration_text: So the procedures now check for themselves. Codes resolve to real I Ds. A key repeated inside one payload is rejected. A line that already exists is either refused, or deliberately overwritten, all inside one transaction. And the smoke tests prove it. Import three lines, import the same three again, and the budget does not move.

show.event: four checks tick in narration order
smoke run 1 lands: 'Import 3 lines' → 3 written
run 2: 'The same 3 again' → 3 rejected · budget unchanged, border terracotta
run 3: 'Unknown code + repeated key' → 3 rejected

checks: repeated keys in a payload: rejected

beats.narration_text: Now the honest part. One. None of this has run against a live Snowflake account yet. A hundred and three tests pass, and not one of them touches a database. Two. Two imports into the same budget at the same moment can still both slip through. Three. Two converted procedures are still placeholders.

show.event: three empty cards; card one fills: 'Not run live yet'
card two fills: 'Concurrent imports'
card three fills: 'Placeholders remain'
all three hold for the read

items.head: Not run live yet
items.body: 103 tests pass, and none of them touches a database. The first real deploy is still ahead.

items.head: Concurrent imports

beats.role_note: FALSIFIABILITY — what has not been proven yet, stated on screen.

beats.narration_text: Let me recap. Compiling on Snowflake is where a migration starts. The linter catches what Snowflake rejects. Parity catches what it quietly changes. Constraints are declared, not enforced, so the code has to enforce them. And the test for all of it: run it twice. If anything doubles, it is not migrated yet.

show.event: artifact card springs in
heading settles
four verdict lines stagger in, one per spoken clause
the card holds full for the read

artifactLines: Compiling on Snowflake is where a migration starts, not where it ends.
Lint catches what Snowflake rejects; parity catches what it quietly changes.
Constraints are declared, not enforced — so the code has to enforce them.
The test: run it twice. If anything doubles, it is not migrated.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Take one stored procedure from your own migration, and paste this. List every place it relies on the old engine to enforce something the new engine only declares: a unique key, a foreign key, a check, an identity value. For each one, show me what happens if the procedure runs twice. That last line is the one that matters. Running it twice is the cheapest test there is, and it is the one migrations skip.
